questions.prompt: DESIGN IT — [senior] offline edits for a planner app: optimistic UI, a mutation queue and conflict handling (master, README.md). Scenario: the day planner grows to 50,000 users who each use a phone and a laptop; commuters edit for up to three hours with no signal, queueing around 40 edits a trip (ticking tasks, extending schedule blocks, logging time); the time log is billed to clients, so a duplicated or lost entry is money; and the same task is often changed on the laptop while the phone is offline. Write your design before you look: what one queued edit is and where it lives, how an edit made offline can refer to something also created offline, what the server does when the same edit arrives twice, how a conflict between the phone and the laptop is detected and resolved, where validation lives for edits that arrive late, what a queued edit should carry (a value or an intent), how the screen updates at once and recovers when the server says no, how replay handles one edit that can never succeed, and how the app decides it is offline. Then tick the checkpoints you covered and add up the weights (suggested pass: 70% with every [w3] hit)

keyPoints.text: [w3] A queued edit is a durable record in IndexedDB (here a Dexie table) with a client-generated UUID, the user, a type, a payload and the time it was queued, and that UUID must be the server's idempotency key: the server records each processed id in the same transaction as the edit and answers a resend with 'already applied'. As built the client generates the id but the server never stores it, so a new time entry or schedule block that is sent again is inserted again.

[w3] Records created offline need ids the client chooses, or later queued edits cannot name them. As built the replay of a new schedule block or time entry lets the database generate the id, and an offline create adds nothing to the cached day, so the commuter cannot see, extend or correct it until they reconnect. Client UUIDs as primary keys (validated as UUIDs on the server) let the item appear at once and let later queued edits name it; the alternative is a temporary-id map that replay rewrites.

[w3] Conflicts are detected with a precondition, not a clock race. As built replay applies last-writer-wins by comparing the row's server-set updatedAt with a client timestamp (the payload's updatedAt if sent, otherwise the time the edit was queued on the device), so a phone whose clock runs five minutes fast wins every conflict. Send the version (or updatedAt) the client last saw; apply when it still matches, and otherwise merge per field or show the conflict.

[w3] Late edits must pass the same rules as live ones. The sync endpoint's zod schema validates only the envelope (id, user, type, createdAt) and accepts the payload as a record of unknown values, and each replay handler casts fields with TypeScript `as`, so none of the route schemas or business checks run on an offline edit. Give each mutation type its own schema and call the same service function from the route and from the replay.

[w2] Queue intent, not a snapshot of the screen. As built the planned-minutes button queues an absolute total computed from the item as rendered, which overwrites whatever the laptop set meanwhile, and extending the selected block queues an 'extend by' amount that only the online route understands. An increment survives concurrent edits but needs the edit id for dedupe, since applying it twice adds twice; a set is safe to resend but needs the version it was based on, or it overwrites the other device.

[w2] Optimistic updates need an undo path. As built a handler patches the cached day before the request, and when the online request fails it shows a toast and refetches the day; the shared hook has no snapshot or rollback of its own. The React Query recipe is onMutate (cancel in-flight fetches, snapshot the cache, patch it), onError (restore the snapshot) and onSettled (invalidate just the affected keys); the hook instead invalidates every query in the app after every successful write.

[w2] Replay is ordered per user and must separate retryable failures from permanent ones. As built the queue is read in queued-time order and each edit is applied in its own transaction; the server returns the failed ids with reasons, but the client only removes the applied ones and ignores the failures, so an edit that can never succeed is retried forever. Retry network and server errors with backoff, move validation and missing-row failures to a 'needs attention' list the user can fix or discard, and hold edits that depend on a failed create.

[w1] The browser's online flag is a weak signal: it reports online behind a captive portal or on dead Wi-Fi. As built an edit is queued only when the flag says offline; if the flag says online and the fetch fails, the hook throws, the optimistic change is already on screen and nothing is queued. Treat the queue as the only write path and drain it immediately when the network allows.

questions.prompt: PRE-MORTEM — the first month of the offline feature. A consultant's client invoice shows two identical 90-minute entries after a train ride through a tunnel; a task's change made on the phone during a three-hour trip vanishes after sync, although the banner said everything synced; a schedule block extended offline is back to its old length; a phone has shown '3 pending' for two weeks; a block created offline overlaps another one, which the online app always refuses; and on a shared family laptop, the previous user's queued edits are still stored after they signed out. What breaks, how does each show up, and what in your design prevents it?

keyPoints.text: [w3] The duplicate entry is a lost response, not a double tap: the server applied the batch, the tunnel cut the reply, the client kept every edit and sent them again on reconnect, and the replay loop remembers what it applied only in a local array for the length of that request, so the time entry was inserted twice. A processed-ids table written in each edit's transaction makes the resend a no-op.

[w3] The vanished change is last-writer-wins doing what it says, silently: the laptop touched the row after the phone queued its edit, so the comparison skips the update and returns without error, the edit is counted as applied and removed from the queue, and nobody is told. Report a skipped edit as a conflict, and keep it until the user sees it.

[w2] The block reverts because the replay's schedule update only reads start, end, task, label and locked, while the edit the client queued carries an 'extend by' amount, so offline the extension is dropped and only the task link is applied. One implementation per mutation type, shared by route and replay, removes this whole class of drift.

[w2] '3 pending' never clears because failures have nowhere to go: the sync call removes only applied ids, the failed list in the response is never read, a thrown request is swallowed to keep the queue, and the badge just recounts the queue. Every failed edit needs a reason the user can see and act on.

[w2] The overlap only happens offline: the online create route rejects blocks that are not on 30-minute boundaries and answers 409 when a block overlaps another, while the replay creates whatever the payload says. Running the route's rules in the replay fixes it, and an overlap found at replay is a conflict to show, not an edit to drop.

[w1] The queue is per browser profile and nothing clears it: sign-out is a plain form post to the logout route, no code ever empties the IndexedDB table, and the next user's sync only sends their own rows, so the previous user's notes and times stay readable on that device. Drain, then clear, on sign-out, and warn if that would discard unsent edits.

questions.prompt: TRADE-OFF HANDBACK — defend your offline design against the alternatives: last-writer-wins versus a version precondition versus per-field merge versus a CRDT; queueing every write versus writing directly when online and queueing only when offline; one batch sync endpoint versus replaying each edit against its normal route; one transaction per edit versus one for the whole batch; optimistic updates versus waiting for the server; and ordering edits by the device's clock versus the server's arrival order. For each, say what you bought and what it cost.

keyPoints.text: [w3] Last-writer-wins is one comparison and silently drops the losing device's change; a version precondition loses nothing but needs a screen that asks the user; merging per field settles most planner clashes by itself (status from the phone, minutes from the laptop) as long as each queued edit lists only the fields it changed; a CRDT library merges everything automatically, a heavy dependency for rows this small.

[w3] Queueing every write gives one code path, one ordering and one place for retries, and costs a short delay even when online; writing directly when online and queueing only offline is faster in the common case but leaves two implementations of every write that drift apart, which is what happened here: the online route and the replay enforce different rules.

[w2] A batch endpoint is one request with a guaranteed order, but it is a second implementation of every write, with its own validation and authorisation to get right; replaying each edit against its normal route reuses all of that at the cost of one request per edit and ordering that the client must enforce.

[w2] A transaction per edit lets 39 of 40 edits land when one is bad, and leaves partial state when later edits depended on the failed one; one transaction for the batch is all-or-nothing, so one bad edit blocks a commuter's whole trip.

[w2] Optimistic updates hide latency and are the only possibility offline, at the cost of rollback code and a visible 'not yet saved' state; waiting for the server is honest and simple, and leaves a spinner on every tick or an app that does nothing without signal.
keyPoints.quote: Offline banner with pending count and sync action

keyPoints.text: [w1] The device clock orders a commuter's own edits correctly but cannot be trusted across devices; the server's arrival order is consistent but puts three hours of offline edits behind everything that arrived meanwhile; per-row version numbers, or a hybrid logical clock, order changes without trusting any wall clock.
